title: Immediate belief is not blind persuasion; moral marks are helps, not de fide proofs
source_text: IX. Deinde, quum dicimus nos immediate Scripturae credere, per internam Spiritus sancti efficaciam, non vero probationis alicujus interventu, sententia nostra non est, fidem nostram de Scriptura sacra esse caecam persuasionem, et quae sui nullam rationem habeat. Neque per id negamus, eum qui Scripturae, sicuti par est, credit, eo adduci quibusdam argumentis, quae viro prudenti suadere possunt Scripturam veram esse, et a Deo profectam. Etenim per vocem illam immediate non excludimus probationes qualescunque, sed solum probationes quas scholae vocant de fide, id est, quae petitae sint ex aliquo fidei principio, et faciant rem esse de fide, et possint per se fidei articulum fundare. Hujusmodi vero non sunt probationes illae quibus Scripturae sacrae divinitas suadetur. Nec enim petuntur ex ullo fidei principio, et ex aliqua fidei regula; sed tantum ex notis et signis variis: et totae constant argumentis quibusdam moralibus, quae per se parere non possunt eam certitudinem quae requiritur in fide: quandoquidem certitudo quae fidei debetur, ex se et ex suo genere, aequat, si non superat, certitudinem omnem quae nasci potest ex demonstratione. Ac proinde, quamvis probationes istae sint fidei adjumenta et credendi motiva, attamen plena fidei certitudo, qua libros sacros amplecti debemus, ad eas referenda non est, tanquam ad proprium atque praecipuum suum fundamentum, sed potius ad internam Spiritus sancti persuasionem.
pass_a_gloss: Next, when we say that we believe Scripture immediately, by the inward efficacy of the Holy Spirit, and not by the intervening of some proof, our meaning is not that our faith concerning sacred Scripture is a blind persuasion and one that has no reason of itself. Nor by that do we deny that he who believes Scripture, as is fitting, is led to that by certain arguments which can persuade a prudent man that Scripture is true and comes from God. For by that word immediately we do not exclude proofs of every kind, but only those proofs which the schools call de fide, that is, which are drawn from some principle of faith, and make the matter to be of faith, and can by themselves found an article of faith. But of that kind are not those proofs by which the divinity of sacred Scripture is urged. For they are not sought from any principle of faith, and from some rule of faith; but only from various notes and signs: and they entirely consist of certain moral arguments, which of themselves cannot produce that certainty which is required in faith: seeing that the certainty owed to faith, of itself and of its kind, equals, if it does not surpass, every certainty that can be born from demonstration. And therefore, although those proofs are helps of faith and motives of believing, yet the full certainty of faith by which we ought to embrace the sacred books is not to be referred to them, as to its proper and chief foundation, but rather to the inward persuasion of the Holy Spirit.
pass_b_english: Next, when we say we believe Scripture immediately by the Spirit's inward efficacy, not by some proof stepping in between, we do not mean that our faith about sacred Scripture is a blind persuasion with no reason of its own.
Nor do we deny that the person who believes Scripture as he should is led there by arguments that can persuade a prudent mind that Scripture is true and comes from God.

By that word immediately we shut out only the proofs the schools call de fide — proofs drawn from some principle of faith, that make a matter of faith, and that can by themselves found an article of faith — not every kind of proof whatever.

The arguments that urge sacred Scripture's divinity are not of that kind. They are not taken from any principle or rule of faith, but only from various notes and signs, and they consist wholly of moral arguments that cannot of themselves yield the certainty faith requires — for the certainty owed to faith equals, if it does not surpass, every certainty demonstration can produce.

So although those proofs are helps to faith and motives for believing, the full certainty by which we ought to embrace the sacred books is not to be referred to them as its proper and chief foundation, but rather to the Spirit's inward persuasion.
